en: Now, when it comes to the number of
parameters, there is one special case, one
special scenario,
and that would be functions like this,
a sumUp function, which simply sums up all
the values we pass in.
We can have functions like this,
and even though this function takes 6
parameters, 6 arguments in this case, I
would argue that it's very easy to read and
understand. It's very clear what this
function does,
and the order does actually not matter here
even for this example. Still, technically,
we violate the rule of having less than or
equal to 3 parameters. Here we have 6.
Now, of course, we could rewrite this
function,
also internally, of course, to take an array
as an argument. Then we technically have
only 1 argument because this is 1 array.
Please note the square brackets.
We could do this and this could be a
perfectly viable solution.
But we don't even have to do that.
So here I'll comment it out so that we still
have it for reference. Otherwise, of course,
we learned that we shouldn't comment out
things but simply delete them.
Nonetheless, here I'm doing it so that we
still have this alternative solution for
comparison.
But I still want to make a point that this
way of doing it also can be absolutely fine
because most programming languages allow you
to take in a dynamic number of arguments,
and they then have a certain syntax for
grouping all these arguments together into
an array
inside of that function.
For example, here in JavaScript, it's this
3-dot
operator here,
which simply tells JavaScript that numbers
can be any number of parameters,
any number of values, but that they will all
be merged together into one array.
Which is why then we can simply loop through
that array to do something with the values
in there.
And that allows us to define a function
which technically takes more than one
parameter and more than 3 parameters even,
but which still is very readable and
internally simply uses an array.
And I would argue that functions like this
also are pretty clean because ultimately we
must not forget that clean code is not about
hard rules which you have to follow under
all circumstances,
but that it's about writing code which is
understandable, easy to read, and easy to
maintain.
And this code is perfectly easy to read and
maintain. Hence, there is nothing wrong with
it.
